prompt: `internal/demo/demo.go` holds `//go:generate touch made-by-generate`. Ana runs `go build ./...` and then `ls internal/demo`. What does she see?
hint: Which command reads the directives?

choices.text: Only `demo.go`; a build compiles the package and never runs a directive
choices.why: Right. `go build` compiles and never runs a directive; the file appeared only after `go generate ./...`.

choices.text: `demo.go` and `made-by-generate`
choices.why: That assumes a build runs the directives before it compiles, which is how `make` works, not the go command. `go help generate` says it is never run automatically by `go build` or `go test`.

choices.text: A build error, because a package may not contain directives that `go build` cannot run
choices.why: A directive is a comment to the compiler. The package built and printed nothing.

choices.text: `demo.go` and `made-by-generate`, written to the build cache rather than the package
choices.why: Nothing ran, so nothing was written anywhere. The cache holds compiled packages, not a directive's output.

prompt: In `~/gen-try`, the file `internal/demo/demo.go` holds `//go:generate pwd`. Ana types `go generate ./...` at the top of the module. What does `pwd` print?
hint: Where does go generate start each command?

choices.text: `/home/ana/gen-try`, the directory she typed the command in
choices.why: A shell would start the command there. go generate changes to the package's directory first.

choices.text: `/home/ana/gen-try/internal/demo`
choices.why: Right. A directive runs in the directory of the package that holds it, so its relative paths are relative to that file.

choices.text: The module cache directory, where the go command keeps sources
choices.why: The module cache holds downloaded modules. Your own package runs where it lives.

choices.text: A temporary directory, so that a generator cannot touch the source tree
choices.why: `touch made-by-generate` left its file next to `demo.go`; nothing isolates a generator from the tree.

prints each command, then runs it

prompt: What does `go tool stringer -type=Class` write when it runs from the directive in `internal/status/class.go`?
hint: Look at the file name it produced and the one method in it.

choices.text: A `String() string` method for `Class`, in `class_string.go`
choices.why: Right. It reads the constants of type `Class` and writes the method that names them, in a file named after the type.

choices.text: A new version of `class.go` with a `String` method added at the end
choices.why: stringer never edits your file. Its output goes in a separate file, so regenerating cannot damage what you wrote.

choices.text: The `Class` constants, numbered from the names listed in the directive
choices.why: It goes the other way: you write the constants, and stringer reads them.

choices.text: A test file that checks every constant prints its name
choices.why: There is no test; the check it does write is the `func _()` guard, which the compiler runs.

prompt: stringer wrote `_Class_name = "InformationalSuccessRedirectionClientErrorServerError"` and `_Class_index = [...]uint8{0, 13, 20, 31, 42, 53}`. How many bytes long is the name `String` returns for `Redirection`, the third constant?
hint: The third name runs from the third number to the fourth.

prompt: Ana changes `Informational Class = iota + 1` to `Informational Class = iota` and runs `go build ./...` without regenerating. What happens?
hint: Every constant drops by one, and `func _()` indexes a one-element array with each.

choices.text: The build succeeds, and `Success` prints as `Informational`
choices.why: That would be the result without the guard. With it, the stale file never compiles.

choices.text: stringer runs again by itself, since its file is out of date
choices.why: Nothing runs stringer but `go generate`; `go build` only compiles what is there.

choices.text: A panic the first time `String` is called on a `Class`
choices.why: The failure comes earlier: the indices are constants, so the compiler checks them.

choices.text: It fails to compile: each index in `class_string.go` is now -1
choices.why: Right. `x[Informational-1]` became `x[-1]`, and the compiler refused all five lines with `must not be negative`.

prompt: A colleague appends `Nonstandard` to the constant block, after `ServerError`, so it gets the value 6, and does not run `go generate`. What do `go build` and `fmt.Println(status.Nonstandard)` do?
hint: The guard lists the constants stringer saw when it ran.

choices.text: The build fails, because the guard checks every constant of the type
choices.why: The guard has one line per constant it saw, and `Nonstandard` is not among them, so nothing checks it.

choices.text: It builds, and `String` falls back to printing `Class(6)`
choices.why: Right. No existing value moved, so every index is still 0; `String` finds 6 past the end of its table and falls back to the number.

choices.text: It builds, and prints `ServerError`, the last name in the table
choices.why: The range check in `String` stops any index past the last name; it never reuses one.

choices.text: It builds, and prints an empty string
choices.why: The fallback builds `Class(` plus the number plus `)`, never an empty name.

prompt: Why does `genowners` pass the template's output through `format.Source` before writing it?
hint: Compare the template's map entries with the ones in `owners_gen.go`.

choices.text: To lay the code out as `gofmt` would, and refuse output that is not valid Go
choices.why: Right. The template wrote entries flush left; `format.Source` parsed them, indented them and aligned the values, so `gofmt -l` listed nothing.

choices.text: Because `go build` rejects a file that is not formatted
choices.why: The compiler accepts any layout. Unformatted output fails a formatting check, such as lesson 6's, not the build.

choices.text: To add the `// Code generated` header the template leaves out
choices.why: The header is the first line of the template itself; `format.Source` only reformats.

choices.text: To sort the map entries by path
choices.why: The entries came out in the order of `owners.txt`, `/` first and `/health` last; nothing sorted them.

prompt: The directive in `internal/owner/owner.go` runs `go run example.com/hits/tools/genowners` rather than `go run ../../tools/genowners`. What does the import path buy?
hint: Where does a directive run, and what happens to a relative path when the package moves?

choices.text: `go run` refuses relative paths inside a directive
choices.why: It accepts them; the section says `../../tools/genowners` would also work, today.

choices.text: It downloads genowners from the module proxy at a fixed version
choices.why: `example.com/hits` is the module itself; `go run` builds the generator from the same working tree.

choices.text: The directive still works if the package moves deeper
choices.why: Right. The directive runs in the package's directory, so `../../` depends on its depth; the import path names the same package from anywhere in the module.

choices.text: It sets `$GOPACKAGE`, which a relative path would leave empty
choices.why: go generate sets `$GOPACKAGE` for every directive, whatever command it names.

prompt: A different generator opens its output with `os.Create(out)` first and runs `tmpl.Execute` straight into the file. Its input has a bad line, and `Execute` fails halfway. What is left, and when does anybody notice?
hint: `os.Create` empties the file the moment it opens it.

choices.text: The old file, because `os.Create` keeps the contents until the file is closed
choices.why: `os.Create` truncates on opening. The old contents are gone before the first byte is written.

choices.text: Nothing at all: the go command deletes the output of a failed generator
choices.why: go generate reports the failure and stops the package; it knows nothing about which files a generator wrote.

choices.text: A complete file, because `Execute` writes nothing until the template finishes
choices.why: `Execute` writes as it goes, straight to the writer it was given.

choices.text: Half a Go file; the next build fails inside it
choices.why: Right. The file was emptied, then partly written. That is why `genowners` builds everything in a buffer and writes once, at the end.

prompt: Why are `class_string.go` and `owners_gen.go` committed to the repository rather than listed in `.gitignore`?
hint: Who runs `go generate`, and who never does?

choices.text: Because the go command refuses to build a file that git does not track
choices.why: The go command does not read git's index; it compiled both files before the repository existed.

choices.text: No build runs `go generate`, so a clone or a download gets only what was committed
choices.why: Right. Without them, `owner` does not compile and `classes` prints numbers, on every machine but the author's.

choices.text: So that the header line can be checked by `git diff`
choices.why: `git diff` compares contents; it has no idea what a header means. The header is for tools and people.

choices.text: Because regenerating them on every machine would give each a different file
choices.why: With the same generator version, the output is the same everywhere; the reason is that nobody but the author regenerates.

prompt: Which of these first lines mark a Go file as generated, by the rule in `go help generate`? Choose all that apply.
hint: `^// Code generated .* DO NOT EDIT\.$`, before the first text that is not a comment.

choices.text: `// Code generated by "stringer -type=Class"; DO NOT EDIT.`
choices.why: Yes. It is stringer's own header and matches the expression exactly.

choices.text: `// Code generated by genowners from owners.txt; DO NOT EDIT.`
choices.why: Yes. Any text may stand between `Code generated` and `DO NOT EDIT.`.

choices.text: `// Code generated by genowners; DO NOT EDIT`
choices.why: No full stop at the end, and the expression ends in `\.$`. Tools read this file as handwritten.

choices.text: `/* Code generated by genowners; DO NOT EDIT. */`
choices.why: The expression asks for a line starting with `// `, so a block comment does not match.

prompt: A pull request adds a new directive, and its author never commits the file it writes. CI runs `go generate ./... && git diff --exit-code` and passes. Why?
hint: What does `git diff` compare?

choices.text: The directive is new, so CI has no generator to run
choices.why: go generate ran it in CI and wrote the file; the problem is what the comparison looks at.

choices.text: `git diff` compares tracked files only, and the new file was never added
choices.why: Right. The new file is untracked, so it is not in the diff; `test -z "$(git status --porcelain)"` would have failed.

choices.text: `--exit-code` only fails on changes to files that carry the generated header
choices.why: It fails on any change to a tracked file, generated or not; it knows nothing of headers.

choices.text: go generate skips directives in files that changed in the latest commit
choices.why: go generate reads every directive it finds; it does not look at git history.

prompt: `go fix -diff ./legacy` printed a change to `old.go` only, though `old_gen.go` holds the same `interface{}`. Why was `old_gen.go` left out?
hint: Look at the first line of each file.

choices.text: `go fix` only rewrites functions whose names start with an upper-case letter
choices.why: Both functions, `Echo` and `EchoGen`, are exported; the names are not what differs.

choices.text: Its header marks it generated, and `go fix` skips generated files
choices.why: Right. A fix there would be undone by the next `go generate`, so `go fix` checks `ast.IsGenerated` and leaves it.

choices.text: A file whose name ends in `_gen.go` is not compiled
choices.why: The name is a convention for people; the go command compiled `owners_gen.go` like any other file.

choices.text: `-diff` shows only the first file that would change
choices.why: It shows every change; there was only one to show.

prompt: A colleague adds `-linecomment` to the stringer directive, runs `go build ./...`, sees it pass, and commits without running `go generate`. Which check stops that commit from going unnoticed?
hint: What does the guard in `func _()` compare, and did any of it change?

choices.text: The compiler, through the guard in `func _()`
choices.why: The guard checks constant values, and no value changed: the build passed in the transcript.

choices.text: `go vet`, which compares each header with its directive
choices.why: Nothing in the go command compares a header with a directive; the header is a marker, not a record to check.

choices.text: The CI step that regenerates and runs `git diff --exit-code`
choices.why: Right. It wrote the new `class_string.go`, found it different from the committed one, printed the diff and exited 1.

choices.text: `go test`, because `class_string.go` is out of date
choices.why: `go test` builds what is there, exactly like `go build`, and never runs a directive.

prompt: A service sends a welcome e-mail from an HTML file that the design team edits, and the program fills in a name with `html/template`. Generate Go from the file, or embed it?
hint: Does the program need the file as Go, or as data?

choices.text: Generate, so the compiler checks the HTML
choices.why: The compiler checks Go, not HTML. A generated string literal holding the page would be checked no more than the file is.

choices.text: Generate, because embedded files are read from disk when the program starts
choices.why: `//go:embed` puts the bytes in the binary at build time; nothing is read from disk at run time.

choices.text: Embed: the program needs the bytes, and embedding has nothing to go stale
choices.why: Right. A template is data for `html/template`; `//go:embed` reads the file at every build, so there is no generated copy to forget.

choices.text: Neither: a file edited by another team must be fetched over the network at run time
choices.why: Nothing in the case asks for that, and it would add a failure at run time that both build-time options avoid.
